content: 1. The ONTARGET and TRANSCEND studies evaluated the cardiovascular and renal outcomes of telmisartan, ramipril, or their combination in individuals at high renal risk. These studies provided insights into the comparative efficacy and safety of these therapeutic approaches in managing hypertension and associated complications. 2. A systematic review and meta-analysis by Lu et al. compared the combination therapy of renin-angiotensin system inhibitors with calcium channel blockers against other two-drug combinations for hypertension. The findings highlighted the potential benefits of specific drug combinations in achieving optimal blood pressure control. 3. Cheng et al. conducted a PRISMA-compliant meta-analysis to assess the renoprotective effects of combining renin-angiotensin system inhibitors with either calcium channel blockers or diuretics in hypertensive patients. The study emphasized the importance of tailored therapy to protect renal function in this population. 4. Luthy et al. explored cost-efficient treatment strategies for uninsured or underinsured patients with chronic conditions such as hypertension, depression, diabetes mellitus, insomnia, and gastroesophageal reflux. The study underscored the need for affordable and effective therapeutic options in resource-limited settings. 5. Bramlage and Hasford reviewed the impact of antihypertensive drug treatment on blood pressure reduction, persistence, and associated costs. Their findings highlighted the economic and clinical implications of long-term adherence to antihypertensive therapy. 6. Fixed-dose combination therapies were examined by Chrysant as a strategy to achieve blood pressure goals. The study demonstrated the advantages of such combinations in simplifying treatment regimens and improving patient adherence. 7. Nuckols et al. analyzed the cost-effectiveness of antihypertensive medications, considering race and sex differences using data from the REGARDS study. The findings provided valuable insights into personalized treatment approaches for diverse populations. 8. Hogan et al. evaluated the economic impact of antihypertensive treatment with and without benazepril in patients with chronic renal insufficiency. The study highlighted the cost-effectiveness of specific therapeutic regimens in managing hypertension in this subgroup. 9. Ekwunife et al. conducted a cost-utility analysis of antihypertensive medications in Nigeria, emphasizing the importance of decision analysis in resource-constrained healthcare systems. 10. Schwander et al. compared the cost-utility of eprosartan versus enalapril in primary prevention and nitrendipine in secondary prevention in Europe. The study provided evidence for the economic benefits of specific antihypertensive agents in different clinical scenarios. 11. Chan et al. assessed the cost-effectiveness of amlodipine compared to valsartan in preventing stroke and myocardial infarction among hypertensive patients in Taiwan. The findings supported the use of amlodipine as a cost-effective option in this population. 12. Wrona et al. evaluated the health outcomes and economic consequences of using ACE inhibitors versus ARBs in treating arterial hypertension in Poland. The study highlighted the clinical and economic considerations in selecting antihypertensive agents. 13. The Vietnam Ministry of Health's 2014 Joint Annual Health Review emphasized strengthening prevention and control of non-communicable diseases, including hypertension, as a public health priority. 14. Buckley et al. systematically reviewed beliefs about hypertension and its treatment among African Americans, identifying barriers to effective management and adherence. 15. Alsabbagh et al. explored the relationship between socioeconomic status and nonadherence to antihypertensive drugs, providing a meta-analysis of the factors influencing medication adherence. 16. Lewis reviewed factors associated with medication adherence in hypertensive Black patients, highlighting the need for culturally sensitive interventions to improve outcomes. 17. Gwadhry-Sridhar et al. assessed the impact of interventions on medication adherence and blood pressure control in patients with essential hypertension, emphasizing the role of adherence in achieving therapeutic goals. 18. Al Ghurair et al. systematically reviewed patient-reported barriers to adherence to antihypertensive medications, using the WHO multidimensional adherence model to identify key challenges. 19. Wetzel et al. examined the role of poor compliance as a cause of inadequate blood pressure control, providing a systematic review of the evidence. 20. Angeli et al. discussed the benefits of fixed-dose combination therapy in hypertension, highlighting its role in improving adherence and achieving blood pressure targets. 21. Mallat et al. compared free versus fixed combination antihypertensive therapy for essential arterial hypertension, demonstrating the advantages of fixed combinations in simplifying treatment regimens. 22. Kawalec et al. conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on the effectiveness of fixed-dose combination therapy in hypertension, supporting its use as a preferred treatment strategy. 23. Du et al. evaluated the impact of fixed-dose versus free-equivalent combination therapies on adherence in hypertension, providing evidence for the superiority of fixed-dose combinations. 24. Krousel-Wood et al. emphasized the importance of medication adherence in achieving blood pressure control and favorable clinical outcomes in hypertensive patients. 25. Arguedas et al. reviewed blood pressure targets in adults with hypertension, providing evidence-based recommendations for optimal management. 26. Murad et al. conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of antihypertensive agents in older adults, highlighting the efficacy and safety of various therapeutic options. 27. Garrison et al. examined blood pressure targets for hypertension in older adults, providing insights into individualized treatment goals. 28. Saiz et al. reviewed blood pressure targets for treating hypertension in individuals with cardiovascular disease, emphasizing the importance of tailored therapy. 29. Cheung et al. evaluated the effects of intensive blood pressure control in chronic kidney disease, providing evidence for the benefits of aggressive management in this population. 30. Birtwhistle et al. compared three-month and six-month follow-up intervals for hypertensive patients managed by family practitioners, demonstrating the impact of follow-up frequency on outcomes. 31. Xu et al. investigated the optimal systolic blood pressure target, time to intensification, and follow-up intervals in hypertension treatment, using a population-based retrospective cohort study. 32. Walker et al. reviewed patient expectations and experiences with remote monitoring for chronic diseases, highlighting the potential of telehealth in hypertension management. 33. Jaana et al. discussed the role of home telemonitoring in hypertension care, emphasizing its benefits in improving self-management and clinical outcomes. 34. Brook and Weder explored the concept of one combination fits most in initial hypertension treatment, advocating for the use of combination therapies in achieving blood pressure goals. 35. Greer et al. systematically reviewed pharmacist-led chronic disease management, comparing its effectiveness and harms with usual care in hypertension management. 36. Conn et al. reviewed interventions to improve medication adherence in hypertensive patients, providing evidence for the effectiveness of various strategies. 37. Reeves et al. evaluated pharmacist interventions in managing blood pressure control and adherence to antihypertensive medications, demonstrating their impact on clinical outcomes. 38. Morrissey et al. analyzed the effectiveness and content of interventions to enhance medication adherence and blood pressure control in hypertension, providing a systematic review and meta-analysis. 39. Ruppar et al. reviewed medication adherence interventions among hypertensive Black adults, emphasizing the need for targeted strategies to address disparities. 40. Xu et al. evaluated interventions to improve medication adherence among Chinese patients with hypertension, providing a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. 41. Georgiopoulos et al. highlighted the nurse's role in alleviating nonadherence to hypertension treatment, emphasizing the importance of nursing interventions in improving outcomes. 42. Tucker et al. reviewed the impact of self-monitoring of blood pressure on medication adherence and lifestyle factors, providing evidence for its role in hypertension management. 43. Fletcher et al. examined the effect of self-monitoring of blood pressure on medication adherence and lifestyle changes, supporting its use as a complementary strategy in hypertension care. 44. Reboussin et al. conducted a systematic review for the 2017 ACC/AHA guidelines on hypertension management, providing evidence-based recommendations for prevention, detection, and treatment. 45. Sheppard et al. reviewed self-monitoring of blood pressure in patients with hypertension-related multimorbidity, demonstrating its benefits in improving outcomes. 46. Anand et al. evaluated task-sharing with non-physician healthcare workers for blood pressure management in lowand middle-income countries, providing evidence for its effectiveness in resource-limited settings. 47. Fu et al. examined the association of health literacy with high-quality home blood pressure monitoring in hypertensive patients, emphasizing the role of education in improving self-management. 48. Beyhaghi and Viera compared the cost-effectiveness of clinic, home, and ambulatory blood pressure measurement for hypertension diagnosis, providing insights into optimal diagnostic strategies. 49. Jamshidnezhad et al. reviewed the effects of smartphone applications on self-care in hypertensive patients, highlighting the potential of mobile health technologies in improving adherence and outcomes. 50. Marquez-Contreras et al. evaluated the efficacy of a home blood pressure monitoring program on therapeutic compliance in hypertension, demonstrating its impact on adherence and blood pressure control. 51. Jacob et al. reviewed the economics of team-based care in controlling blood pressure, providing evidence for its cost-effectiveness in community settings. 52. Kulchaitanaroaj et al. conducted a cost-utility analysis of physician-pharmacist collaborative interventions for hypertension treatment, supporting their use as a cost-effective strategy. 53. Zhao et al. reviewed the efficacy of empowerment strategies for hypertensive patients, emphasizing the importance of patient-centered approaches in improving outcomes. 54. Parati and Omboni discussed the role of home blood pressure telemonitoring in hypertension management, providing an update on its benefits and challenges. 55. Choi et al. reviewed mobile health technologies for self-management of concurrent diabetes and hypertension, highlighting their potential in improving outcomes in patients with comorbid conditions. 56. McKoy et al. evaluated the effectiveness and risks of telehealth technologies for hypertension care and self-management, providing insights into their clinical and economic implications. 57. Cheema et al. reviewed the impact of pharmacist interventions in community pharmacies on hypertension control, demonstrating their effectiveness in improving adherence and outcomes. 58. Lin et al. compared the effects of calcium channel blockers with ACE inhibitors and ARBs in hypertensive patients with chronic kidney disease stages 3 to 5 and those on dialysis, providing a systematic review and meta-analysis of their efficacy and safety.
